nameStory: The 'cryptops' part of this centipede's name comes from Greek words meaning 'hidden eye,' referring to how their eyes are tucked away and hard to spot. The 'common' part simply means this is the most widespread species in its genus, though with only 13 recorded sightings in New England, it's not exactly what most people would call common!
description: The Common Cryptops is a medium-sized centipede that belongs to the bark centipede family. These golden-brown to reddish arthropods have long, segmented bodies with 21 pairs of legs and can grow to about 1-2 inches long. Unlike the giant centipedes you might see in tropical pet stores, these are much smaller and spend most of their time hidden under bark, logs, or stones where they hunt tiny insects and other small prey.

idTips.label: Body segments and legs
idTips.description: Count 21 body segments, each with one pair of long, thin legs that feel surprisingly delicate if you gently handle one with tweezers

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Golden-brown to rusty orange body that may appear almost translucent in bright light, with legs that are often slightly paler than the body

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Slender, worm-like body about 1-2 inches long that feels firm but flexible, much like a small rubber tube when handled

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Moves in smooth, flowing waves rather than the jerky scuttling of house centipedes, and can quickly disappear into tiny crevices

idTips.label: Head features
idTips.description: Small, dark head with inconspicuous eyes and long, thread-like antennae that constantly probe ahead as it moves

habitat: Look for Common Cryptops under loose bark of dead or dying trees, especially oak and maple, in mixed hardwood forests throughout New England. They also hide under fallen logs, flat stones, and leaf litter in moist areas where the soil stays consistently damp but not waterlogged. You'll have the best luck finding them in mature forests with plenty of decaying wood rather than in young or disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm, often found under bark that's starting to loosen from winter freeze-thaw cycles. This is when they're easiest to spot as they hunt for newly active small insects.
seasonality.summer: Present but often deeper in hiding spots during hot, dry periods. Check under logs and stones in the coolest, most humid microclimates of the forest.
seasonality.fall: Active again as temperatures cool and moisture returns. Often found with their tiny white eggs in protected spaces under bark or stones.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in protected crevices, under thick bark, or in soil. Rarely seen on the surface, but occasionally found during warm spells if you search thoroughly.

funFact: Despite being called 'bark centipedes,' Common Cryptops are actually miniature ambush predators that can inject venom through their front legs (called forcipules) to paralyze prey much larger than you'd expect - they've been observed taking down springtails, small spiders, and even other centipedes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small millipedes, but remember the simple rule: centipedes have one pair of legs per segment and move fast, while millipedes have two pairs per segment and move slowly. If it races away when you lift its hiding spot, it's probably a centipede!
contextualKnowledge: The name 'bark centipede' can be misleading since many centipede species live under bark - it's actually the family name (Cryptopidae) rather than a description of this species' unique habitat. These centipedes are part of the order Scolopendromorpha, which includes some of the world's largest centipedes, though our New England species are much more modest in size.
compareHints: Common Cryptops can be distinguished from its close relative Cryptops leucopodus by its more golden-brown coloration, whereas leucopodus tends to be paler and more yellowish. Both species have the same number of leg pairs and similar size, but Common Cryptops is more likely to be found under deciduous tree bark, while leucopodus prefers coniferous forest habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Common Cryptops, the white-footed cave centipede is generally paler throughout with more pronounced light-colored legs that contrast sharply with the body.
